problem: Quaker wanted to expand its beverage business beyond Gatorade.
title: Quaker Oats buys Snapple for $1.7 billion and sells it for $300 million
context: Snapple was a fast-growing alternative beverage brand, but analysts thought the price was too high.
decision_made: Acquire Snapple in late 1994 for $1.7 billion.
action_taken: Sold Snapple to Triarc for $300 million in 1997, about 27 months later.
observed_outcome: Quaker took a non-cash pretax charge of about $1.4 billion on the sale. Analysts blamed slowing category growth and competition from Coca-Cola and PepsiCo. Chairman William Smithburg resigned in April 1997.
lessons: Paying a premium for a fast-growing brand can fail when growth slows and large rivals respond.
limitations: The final closing loss was reported as $10.6 million in a later filing, since most of the loss was already recorded earlier. Causes are analyst opinion.

claims.claim_text: Quaker bought Snapple for $1.7 billion in late 1994 and agreed to sell it to Triarc for $300 million in 1997.
Quaker recorded a non-cash pretax charge of about $1.4 billion on the sale.
